title: TCP: shake hands, then talk
intro: Before your browser sends a single byte, TCP makes the two computers agree. How many messages?

predict.question: How many messages must be exchanged before the first real data can be sent?
predict.reveal: Three: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. After that both sides know the other is listening and the connection is open.

takeaway: TCP spends a three-step handshake to make delivery reliable; UDP skips it and just sends.

steps.say: Two computers, no connection yet. The server is listening; the browser is closed.
Step 1: the browser says SYN, meaning 'I want to talk, and my numbering starts at 100'.
Step 2: the server answers SYN-ACK: 'Heard you. I am ready, and my numbering starts at 300.'
Step 3: the browser confirms with ACK. Now both sides know the other can hear them.
The connection is open, so the browser can finally send its request.
The server replies with the page. TCP numbers every byte so lost ones can be resent.
To finish, the browser sends FIN: 'I have nothing more to send.'
The server acknowledges, then sends its own FIN because it is done too.
The browser sends a last ACK. The server closes at once; the browser waits a bit in TIME-WAIT in case that ACK got lost.
Reliable, ordered, and a bit slow to start. UDP skips all of this: just send and hope.
